### Observed differences

- The elapsed time between the completion of A28 and the completion of A33 roughly halved. In the earlier window these intervals averaged about 0.9 hours (median about 0.9 hours); in the later window they averaged about 0.46 hours (median about 0.46 hours), a decrease of about 0.45 hours. [TWAIT001]
- The shift affected the whole distribution, not just one part of it: the middle half of the intervals moved from roughly 0.82–0.99 hours to roughly 0.42–0.50 hours, and the spread narrowed from a standard deviation of about 0.13 hours to about 0.06 hours, so intervals in the later window are both shorter and more uniform. [TWAIT001]
- The difference is large relative to random variation: it exceeds what random re-splits of the pooled data produce in more than 99.9% of 2,000 reference comparisons. [TWAIT001]
- The interval was observed somewhat less often in the later window: 58 timing observations versus 45, with both windows containing 200 traces. [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a change in timing: in the later window, the elapsed time between the completion of A28 and the completion of A33 is about half of what it was in the earlier window, with the entire interval distribution shifted down by roughly 0.45 hours rather than only its tail. The change is shown directly by the timing indicator for this activity pair, all distribution components (mean, median, quartiles, spread) move coherently in the same direction, and the observation base is reasonable (58 and 45 intervals). The screening context also fits: the time family produced 1 qualifying item where about 0.01 — roughly 1 in 100 — would be expected if nothing had changed, while the control-flow family produced none (0 items against about 0.28 expected from 57 units), so this single item is far above what chance would produce for its own family. [TWAIT001]

Limitations: the hypothesis rests on a single indicator, and TWAIT measures elapsed time between consecutive completion events rather than pure waiting or processing time, so the decrease could partly reflect changes in what happens between A28 and A33 rather than a pure change in the timing of the interval itself. An important competing explanation the evidence cannot fully rule out is a rare fluctuation of an unchanged process, which still produces such an item in roughly 1 in 100 screenings. [TWAIT001]

Other differences: the consecutive A28–A33 completion pair occurred somewhat less often in the later window (58 versus 45 observations, about 29 versus 23 per 100 traces); this modest participation change did not qualify as a control-flow difference and is not part of the main hypothesis. [TWAIT001]
